1:
The route and the halts are worked out in some detail. Gill notes that between Elim and this wilderness they came again to the Red Sea, probably to some bay or creek in their way, where they camped briefly and recollected what had been done for them there; the stay was short and the narrative passes it over. Ellicott argues from the calendar: the wilderness of Sin was reached exactly a month after leaving Egypt, yet with only five camping-places and one three-day march through a desert, which indicates long rests — probably at Ayun Musa, at Marah and at Elim. The named places, he adds, were only the camp’s headquarters, since the host must always have covered a vast tract with its flocks driven into every valley that had pasture. For the gathering itself he wants open ground, and finds a coastal tract twenty miles long and three or four wide, reached by descending to the shore and continuing south — a line of march he supports from the itinerary in Numbers, which puts an encampment by the Red Sea between Elim and Sin.

Keil and Delitzsch argue against a rival route. Some suppose the Israelites went inland by a road entering the mountains, but that is hard to reconcile with a camp said to lie in the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, since the direct road from Elim to Sinai never touches that plain but turns north-east away from it. One scholar tries to save the route by taking the clause not as locating the desert but as marking where the road crosses it, which they object is contrary to the natural sense and gains nothing.

What the people had been living on, and why it ran out, is answered by three of them. Wesley states it flatly: a month’s provision carried out of Egypt on the fifteenth of the first month, spent by the fifteenth of the second. Henry says the same, and Gill adds a Targum’s note that the dough gave out that very day, having lasted thirty days on the unleavened cakes. Calvin is less sure: some conjecture flour brought from Egypt, but he thinks other food was used too, since the country was not so barren as to yield no fruits or herbs, and the battle with Amalek suggests inhabited land nearby. It was when they went deeper into the desert and lost all commerce with the inhabitants that provision failed, which is why hunger pressed harder and the sedition grew.

On the murmuring itself the readers are severe in different keys. Ellicott counts it the third — the first at Pi-hahiroth when Pharaoh’s host appeared, the second at Marah over the water — and observes that this one had no particular occasion beyond the exhaustion of the grain, but came of a general dissatisfaction with wilderness life and the prospect ahead. Clarke takes it as proof of a degraded mind, and argues that a people so carnal could never have been induced to leave Egypt without striking miracles; human nature sinks no lower than when the body is enslaved and the soul debased by sin, and these were both slaves and sinners. Calvin points out that the remedy was obvious and neglected. They should have prayed to a God they had found a bountiful Father; had they only believed that the earth is made fertile by his blessing, it would have occurred to them that feeding the hungry is his particular office. Instead unbelief betrays itself in turbulent clamour: want, which invited them to feel the power that made the world out of nothing, was met with despair, and they quarrelled with Moses and called their deliverers their murderers. Gill and Wesley note whom the complaint fell on, God’s vicegerents rather than God, and Gill excepts a few, Caleb and Joshua among them, from the whole congregation.
3:
The wish is examined word by word. Ellicott notes there is no mention of God in the Hebrew at all — it is simply would that we had died — and hears in the phrase about the Lord’s hand a possible allusion to the last of the plagues: would we had not been spared but smitten like the Egyptians, since a sudden death is far better than a lingering one. Wesley makes the same point as a charge. They so undervalue their deliverance that they wish they had died in Egypt, and died by the hand of the Lord too, that is by one of the plagues that cut off the Egyptians, as though it were the hand of Moses only that had brought them into this wilderness; and he adds the observation that people commonly call whatever pain they cannot trace to a second cause the pleasure of God, as if what comes by human hand or visible accident were not equally so.

Whether they had ever eaten as well as they claim is disputed. Ellicott says they had: the Israelites were nourished on flesh, fish, bread and abundant vegetables — cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic — since it was the habit of Egyptians to feed well those employed in forced labour, as slave-owners commonly do, and the memory of that plenty sharpened the present want. Wesley flatly denies it. We cannot suppose they had any great plenty in Egypt, however largely they now talk of the fleshpots; discontent magnifies what is past and vilifies what is present without regard to truth or reason, and none talk more absurdly than murmurers. Clarke splits the difference by explaining the image: as slaves they were doubtless fed in companies by their taskmasters at fixed places where large boilers were set up, and the speech proves only that they preferred their bondage to their present state.

Whether starvation was actually near is the harder question. Clarke says they could not have been in absolute want, having brought abundant flocks and herds out of Egypt; Wesley agrees, that they could not fear dying for want while they had their cattle with them. Ellicott works the arithmetic instead and reaches a more complicated answer. It is difficult to imagine any real danger of starvation yet, since the bulk of the cattle survived and there were lambs enough for the whole nation to keep a Passover a few months later; but many Israelites may have had no cattle at all, and others may have lost or consumed theirs, so that want stared some in the face. And even supposing the desert was anciently four or five times as productive as now, it could not have pastured flocks enough to keep two million people on milk and flesh — so the people may have seen their herds visibly diminishing and understood the danger of ultimate starvation once they were gone.

Gill notes only that they did not merely murmur inwardly and privately but spoke their complaint out, and in a very extravagant manner. Keil and Delitzsch carry the text forward without comment to the promise of bread rained from heaven, the daily rate, the proving of the people, and the double portion on the sixth day.
4:
Clarke fastens at once on the word rain and draws a conclusion from it: this substance was therefore not a natural product of the desert, nor was the dew that produced it common there, since otherwise they would have had this bread for a month already. Ellicott presses the same phrase further. The announcement itself suggests a supernatural supply, and bread from heaven means not simply food out of the air but a celestial, that is a divine, provision of daily needs; the rate appointed is literally a day’s meal each day, enough for a man and his household. Wesley builds the contrast into a type: man was made out of the earth and his Maker has wisely ordered his food out of the earth, but Israel, standing for the church of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven and who receive their charters and laws from heaven, receive their food from there too. Gill supposes that Moses had been praying, as was his custom when the people complained, and was heard and answered.

What the trial consists in divides the readers, and Calvin reports the division. Some understand it to mean that God, by kindly providing food, would bind the people to obedience by his own bounty — as if to say, I will try whether they are altogether intractable, for nothing shall be wanting to keep them in the way of duty. Others confine it to the daily allowance, making the test whether they would desire no more than was given and be content with a day’s provision, and so depend on providence. Calvin prefers the first. Ellicott takes a version of the second and generalises it into a doctrine of probation: human life is a probation, God tries most those he takes for his peculiar people, and the trial is often by positive precepts, which are especially calculated to test the presence or absence of humble and unquestioning obedience. He runs the pattern through Scripture — our first parents tested by a positive precept in Paradise, Abraham’s family by circumcision on the eighth day, Israel by many such precepts of which this was one, and Christians by precepts about common worship, prayer and the sacraments — the object in every case being to see whether men will walk in God’s law or no, since men are very apt to prefer their own inventions to the plain letter and spirit of his commandments. Wesley states the same purpose in two words, whether they will trust him and whether they will be faithful to so good a master.

Calvin thinks something has been left out of the narrative. It is not consistent, he says, that such insolence was passed over without a single word of chastisement; God in his extraordinary kindness gave food to depraved men unworthy of the sunlight and the common air, yet he cannot have fostered their sin by silence, and while pardoning their ingratitude must have sharply reproved them. Moses passes over the rebuke to reach the story more worth telling, how God fed this wretched people with bread from heaven when he made the manna fall like dew from the clouds. Calvin defends that title from the psalm which extols God’s bounty as though the people had been admitted to the tables of angels, and distinguishes it from the apostle’s calling the manna spiritual meat, which was said in another sense, because it was a type of the flesh of Christ that feeds our minds to the hope of eternal life; the psalmist makes no allusion to that mystery but turns the circumstance into an accusation, since the people not only despised the food that springs from the earth but grew disgusted even with bread for which they saw the heavens opened.
5:
Ellicott raises a chronological difficulty about the sixth day. He reads it as the sixth day after the manna first fell, and points out how little support there is for a week of named days at this period: a sabbath was kept in Babylonia on the seventh, fourteenth, twenty-first and twenty-eighth of each month from a date earlier than the exodus, but there is no evidence that the year was divided into weeks, still less that the days were known as first, second, third and so on, and in Egypt the seven-day week was at this time unknown. Gill assumes the week without argument, dating the sixth day from a raining of bread that began on the first day of the week — which leaves the two of them disagreeing not about the arithmetic but about whether the reckoning existed to be used.

Whether the doubled portion is a command or a promise is disputed. Some take it as an instruction, that they shall gather twice as much; Ellicott thinks it more natural as an announcement of fact — you will find that what you have gathered turns out to be twice as much — and reports three scholars for that reading, taking a miraculous doubling of the quantity to be intended.

Calvin uses the verse to settle what the proving of the previous verse meant, and rejects a narrow reading of it. Some, he says, because the sabbath is mentioned immediately after, confine the whole trial to its observance, making the experiment whether the people would faithfully keep the rest enjoined every seventh day; but there is a poorness in that explanation. What is actually happening is that God, having promised daily supplies, now adds the exception, that on the sixth day they should collect double and lay half aside for the sabbath. From this Calvin draws a conclusion about the day itself: the seventh was really hallowed before the Law was promulgated, since a provision is being made here for a rest that the Law had not yet enjoined. Whether the patriarchs had already observed it he thinks probable but declines to make a matter of contention, which is a notable restraint in a writer who is otherwise willing to press the point against opponents.
6:
The pair of announcements is read as an answer to the specific taunt. Calvin sets it against the complaint of being betrayed by Moses and Aaron: the two answer that God will openly show himself the author of the deliverance, so that no more complaint may be made against his ministers. The reproof is sharp but joined to a promise, since God does not leave the work of his hands unfinished, and the continuance of his favour proves that the same God who carries the work on had begun it. Calvin then distributes the two clauses — the knowledge given in the evening refers to the quails, and because the power shone more brightly next day in the manna, Moses says that in the morning they should see the glory. He guards against a wrong inference: this was not given them in return for their deserts, but was God contending with their obstinacy, appearing so that by the brightness of his countenance they might see their own impiety and be filled with shame. And lest they should plead that they had only attacked Moses and Aaron, he explains the disclaimer — what are we? — as a refusal to be separated from God at all, which is why the murmuring is called war against God himself. Clarke reads the same disclaimer plainly: they are only servants obeying commands, and it was not they who brought the people up from Egypt. He adds why a standing miracle was needed at all — after everything they had seen, the people still supposed their coming out was the work of Moses and Aaron, since the miracles already given convinced them only while they lasted and were forgotten as soon as they had passed, so God gave them a daily one in the falling of the manna to keep the proof constantly before their eyes.

What the glory means divides them. Ellicott refers it to the manna, which lay round the host in the morning, and not to the appearance in the cloud, which preceded the quails and is not said to have been in the morning at all; the glory was strikingly revealed, he says, in a gift that was not transient but secured the people’s subsistence as long as they needed to remain in the wilderness. Clarke reads it in the cloud and takes a further step. Does the glory not appear here as something distinct from the Lord, since it is the glory that hears the murmuring against the Lord? He grants that the antecedent may simply stand for the relative, but sets the phrase beside the apostle’s description of a Son who is the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person, and infers that since no man has seen God at any time, Christ was the visible agent in all the miraculous interferences of the patriarchal age and under the law. Gill takes the same view, identifying the glory with the Shechinah, the Angel who went before them in the cloud, the eternal Word.
9:
Clarke asks what place the people were summoned to. Coming near before the Lord has been supposed to mean some particular spot where his presence was manifested; but the great tabernacle was not yet built, that portable temple being set up only on the first day of the first month of the second year, more than ten months after this. There seems to have been a smaller tent, the tabernacle of the congregation, which after the sin of the calf was always pitched outside the camp and to which everyone who sought the Lord went out. A further difficulty comes later in the chapter, where an omer of manna is ordered laid up before the testimony, which implies an ark or shrine already existing; if the great tabernacle is meant there, the account of laying up the manna must be introduced by anticipation, Moses finishing a story of what was done afterwards because its reasons arose now. His own preference is simpler: much unbelief still reigned, and to convince them that God and not Moses had brought them out they were told to draw near and attend to an extraordinary manifestation — which he connects with the later word that the Lord would come in a thick cloud so the people might hear and believe Moses for ever.

Calvin reads the summons as a citation to a tribunal. Moses is calling them up as criminals before God, as if to say they were mistaken in thinking their murmurs unobserved; and he alludes at the same time to the cloud, the visible symbol of a presence they did not hesitate to provoke though it stood almost before their eyes. Two things follow: they were drawn from their hiding-places so their pride might be broken, and their stupidity was rebuked for not reverencing a God who was present. He then presses the direction: the glory appeared toward the wilderness, by which he understands the less habitable region, since though the country was barren all round there were Amalekites and other tribes on one side. And by the glory he understands not what they saw daily but something manifested in an unusual manner to inspire alarm, because they had grown hardened against the ordinary manifestations.

Ellicott settles the wording: the Hebrew as pointed has in a cloud, but the pillar of cloud is certainly meant, since it was before this they had been told to appear and from this that a radiance streamed out, the object being to rebuke the murmuring and uphold the authority of Moses and Aaron. Wesley calls it simply an extraordinary and sudden brightness. Gill and Clarke both note that Aaron was the speaker, spokesman to the people as he had earlier been to Pharaoh, and Gill notes that the glory broke in before he had well finished.

Calvin adds a note on the order of the narrative: the statement that the Lord had spoken to Moses is put last though it happened first, and he takes it as a causal clause rather than a connective, showing that Moses had done nothing without God’s command but had discharged a minister’s office faithfully, since without such a word he would have been rash to promise what he did. The sum, as before, is that God will vindicate a glory the people had impugned and do good to the unworthy in order to glorify his name. Gill reads the message the same way: the Lord confirms what Moses and Aaron had said and disapproves the murmuring, yet deals kindly rather than resenting it, since having brought them into a wilderness by his own act he would provide for them. Wesley draws the contrast in the closing clause: when God plagued the Egyptians it was to make them know that he is the Lord, and when he provided for Israel it was to make them know that he was their God.
13:
Whether the birds were quails at all has been argued, and Clarke sets the case out. Several learned men, he reports, have supposed they were locusts, one bishop being driven to it by three difficulties: that they came by a wind, that they covered a circle of thirty or forty miles two cubits deep, and that they were spread in the sun to dry. Clarke rejects the identification. They are expressly called flesh in the psalm, which locusts are not; the Greek and Latin versions render the word by names for a large quail; and the phrase about two cubits should be translated not two cubits high but two cubits apart, since quails do not settle on one another as locusts do — and had they lain three feet deep for a day’s journey round the camp, the people could not have spent two days and a night gathering them. The spreading out, he adds, was to dry them in the burning sand for keeping, which is still done in Egypt. He supports the natural history from a traveller who describes vast numbers coming into Egypt in March when the wheat ripens, hiding in the corn until the farmers spread a net and startle them into it.

Ellicott gives the same account without the controversy. The common quail is abundant in the East and migrates from Syria and Arabia in autumn to winter in central Africa, returning in immense masses in the spring; exhausted by the long flight over the Red Sea, the flocks drop to the ground as soon as they reach the coast, so that the birds may be taken by hand or knocked down with sticks. He cites an ancient historian for the people of Arabia Petraea spreading nets near the coast for furlongs together and taking great quantities of quails coming in from the sea, and notes that the flesh is a delicacy throughout the East though unwholesome in quantity. Gill and Wesley agree on the tameness; Gill locates the flight over the Arabian gulf, notes a Targum that calls them pheasants, and observes that here the birds came for one evening only, where later they lasted a whole month.

Calvin reads that difference as the point. When the people afterwards grew weary of the manna and asked for meat, quails were given again, and a terrible punishment fell on their gluttony while the flesh was still in their mouths; here, where they had only complained of wanting food, God satisfied them with flesh once, to show that all kinds and quantities of meat are in his hand. Yet he willed them content with a single sort, since it was not reasonable to comply altogether with unholy desires, and it was good that bounds should be set so they might learn dependence on his will.

Henry takes the two provisions as a pair with different purposes. The evening feast of feathered fowl — not locusts, he says, on the strength of the same psalm — shows that God gives the good things of life not only for necessity but for delight, so that we may serve him cheerfully. The morning manna is daily bread, and Henry presses the discipline: they were to gather a day’s portion in its day and live on daily providence, like the birds of which it is said that what God gives them they gather, not today for tomorrow. He hears the same lesson in the petition for daily bread, and adds that the plain diet teaches temperance and forbids the desire of dainties, reporting a Jewish tradition that the manna suited every palate and a physician’s opinion that so light a food was needed to clear disorders contracted in their bondage. Ellicott ends on the dew, where the Hebrew is literally there was a lying of dew, and takes a heavy fall to be meant.
14:
Ellicott sets out at length the two natural substances the manna has been compared with, and rejects both. One is a deposit from the air that falls indifferently on trees, stones and grass, usually thick and sticky like honey but sometimes concreted into small granular masses; it has been described from antiquity onwards, is called air-honey, and is collected by Arabs and eaten with unleavened cakes as a condiment. It resembles the manna in coming with the dew, in lying generally on the ground, and in melting when the sun reaches a certain power — but it is never found in quantity, falls for only two months in the year, and is wholly unfit to be a man’s principal food. The other is a gum exuded from certain trees where a small insect has punctured the leaves, a dry substance shaken readily from the branches in hard yellowish-white grains that moderns compare to coriander seed. It is this that bears the name manna in the East, used both as a condiment and as a laxative; but it is confined to particular trees, is comparatively permanent, accumulating on the leaves, is unfit for food, and has only a season of two months. Calvin dismisses the same identification more briskly, as the idle talk of profane persons who would convict Moses of extolling a trifle. It is true that white grains are collected in certain parts of the world and vulgarly called manna, but it is no food, does not drop daily from the clouds, and has nothing in common with what the prophet dignifies as angels’ food. Calvin then lists the marks of a miracle: it did not appear before the hour God had assigned through Moses, and no change of weather — frost, rain, heat, winter or summer — ever interrupted the regular measure of its falling.

Clarke observes the order of the two falls. The dew came first and the substance fell on it, and he supposes the dew was meant to cool the ground so that the manna should not dissolve on landing, since we are told the sun’s heat melted it; the ground being cooled, it lay long enough for a day’s supply to be gathered. Calvin describes the shape only, dew condensed into small round grains, and Gill accounts for the dew’s disappearance simply, exhaled by the sun as it rose. Keil and Delitzsch turn to the measure: everyone was to gather according to the needs of his household, a bowl a head, which the closing verse makes the tenth part of an ephah.
15:
The name is the chapter’s hardest word, and four answers are given. Clarke calls the English a most unfortunate translation which not only gives no sense but contradicts itself, since the text says they did not know what it was and therefore could not have named it; the Hebrew is literally what is this?, which is how almost all the older versions render it, and Moses answers the question at once. He adds that the substance was later called by that name in commemoration of the question, and argues that it was created for the occasion, unknown to their fathers and never seen again after the supply ceased. Ellicott agrees the English is certainly wrong and then objects to Clarke’s rendering as well, since the word does not mean what in Hebrew but only in Chaldee, and what is this would be a very strange name for a substance; he reports four scholars for this is a gift, granting that the word is not found elsewhere in Hebrew in that sense while noting that it has it in Arabic and that a related Hebrew verb means to give. Calvin offers two derivations of his own — a prepared thing, or an assigned portion, preferring the first — but concedes that in Syriac and Chaldee the word is incontestably what, and that the Greek and Latin translators render it so.

Calvin then reads the naming as half-gratitude. By calling it a prepared thing they confessed they were dealt with bountifully, food being presented without labour, and so indirectly condemned their own murmuring, since gathering prepared food is much better than winning it by troublesome culture of the earth. But because unbelief had clouded their senses, Moses adds that they did not know what it was, which rebukes their slowness: forewarned of the miracle, they were astonished as if they had heard nothing of it. Their gratitude was clouded with ignorance, and the reproof is bitter when Moses has to tell them that this was the very food God had promised — for had they recognised the promise fulfilled there would have been no need to recall it. Gill notes that they were up early to look, having been told they should have bread to the full, and Wesley describes what they found: a food that came down in dew and melted, yet was of such consistency as to nourish without anything else, palatable to every taste and light of digestion.
16:
Clarke uses the mention of the omer to set out the whole Hebrew scale of dry and liquid measure. The omer, from a root meaning to press or bind together, whence a sheaf, held about three quarts English and was probably so named as the smallest dry measure the ancient Hebrews knew, the smaller kab appearing only in a later reign. The ephah, from a root meaning to bake and so probably the quantity baked at one time, held some seven gallons and a half. He runs on through the kab, the homer — a different word and the largest of all, ten ephahs, perhaps named from the ass whose ordinary load it was — the bath, always used of liquids, the seah, the hin and the log. Ellicott is content with the omer and turns it into arithmetic: about three pints English, literally for every head, so a family of four would need six quarts, and if five hundred thousand men gathered that the daily supply must have exceeded ninety thousand bushels. Calvin declines the calculation: an omer is the tenth of an ephah, and one might work out its proportion to modern measures, but he will not dispute an unnecessary point, since it is enough to be sure that not less was given than amply sufficed.

The rule itself is read as a discipline. Ellicott says each man was to gather according to his immediate need and his family’s, and nobody was to seek to accumulate a store. Calvin notes that a daily measure is prescribed with an exception to follow for the sabbath, and that God’s liberality extended far enough to satisfy them abundantly. Gill treats the gathering allegorically as believers going out of the camp and out of themselves to Christ, and the unequal amounts as the different degrees of faith, since some are strong and others weak.

How the equality came about is the question. Clarke gives a natural explanation: every man gathered as much as he could, and when it was measured any surplus went to a family that had not managed enough — a large household, or one whose members were too confined to collect for themselves, the cool hours being short. So there was an equality, and Clarke reads the apostle’s use of the verse in that light. Calvin gives essentially the same account and states it more carefully: they did not each collect a private store, but when all had helped they took their prescribed portion from the common heap, so that the more diligent a man was the more he relieved his slower neighbour without any loss to himself. Ellicott refuses the natural explanation outright. Each man gathered what he supposed would be about an omer a head, some overestimating and some under, but whatever the quantity, when it came to be measured in the camp the result was always the same — just an omer for each — and this result, he says, can only have been miraculous.

Calvin then guards the apostle’s application against a use he thinks it cannot bear. The parallel holds figuratively, but manna came daily almost into their hands without tillage, so it is no wonder God called everyone to an equal share and forbade any to take more. Ordinary food is another matter, since society is preserved by each possessing his own — property acquired by purchase, inheritance or gift and increased in proportion to a man’s diligence — and government requires that each enjoy what belongs to him, so it would be absurd to prescribe the manna’s law for common food. The apostle himself, Calvin adds, makes the distinction wisely, enjoining an equality that arises not from a promiscuous use of property but from the rich giving spontaneously and liberally. Gill and Clarke both explain the unequal gathering by the size of households, Clarke adding those who supplied the infirm.
19:
The prohibition is read by everyone as designed rather than arbitrary. Ellicott says Moses must have been divinely instructed to issue it, and that it was given so that the Israelites might realise their absolute dependence on God for food from day to day and be habituated to complete trust. Clarke says the same and hears the petition of the Lord’s Prayer founded on the circumstance — give us day by day our daily bread. Wesley turns it into a picture: they were to learn to go to bed and sleep quietly though there was not a bit of bread in their tent nor in the whole camp, trusting God with the next day. He then widens it: never was there such a market, where hundreds of thousands were daily furnished without money and without price, nor such an open house as God kept for forty years together; and the same wisdom and goodness that brought food daily out of the clouds brings it yearly out of the earth, and gives us all things richly to enjoy.

Calvin treats the disobedience as a diagnosis. Since God supplied their food as the breast is given to babes, it was perverse unbelief that they would not depend on his providence but sought a store for many days; and it proved their obstinacy that they credited no warning until they had laid up nothing in their houses but a mass of corruption. He then works out how far the case applies to ordinary life. Manna and common food are not altogether alike, but the comparison holds to a point: it is lawful to keep corn and wine in granaries and cellars provided all still truly ask their daily bread of God. That will be so, he says, if the rich do not swallow whatever they can get together, gorge themselves on the hunger of the poor or accumulate immoderately, but are liberal out of present abundance, unanxious about the future, untroubled if their wealth should shrink, and glory not in abundance but rest on the fatherly bounty of God. And we often see, he adds, that what misers collect by theft, rapine, fraud, cruelty or meanness turns to corruption in the same way.

What happened to the hoarded portion is read as punishment, not decay. Ellicott makes the argument explicit: the sabbath portion bred no worms at all, so the result must be a penalty for disobedience rather than a natural process, and neither of the natural substances compared with manna decomposes rapidly. Clarke reads it as mercy in a hard form: their sinful curiosity and covetousness led them to make the trial and they had a mass of loathsome putrefaction for their pains, and God is continually making disobedience irksome so that a man may find his evil ways unprofitable and return to his Maker. Keil and Delitzsch put the rule in a sentence — Israel was to take no thought for the morrow but to enjoy the daily bread received from God in obedience to the giver — and note that the gathering had to be in the morning because the manna melted when the sun shone hot.

Calvin ends where the compliance begins, and refuses to call it obedience. When they saw that their intemperate eagerness profited them nothing they submitted to the command; but the submission was not voluntary, being extorted from them, since fools are never wise except after adversity. He reads the melting in the sun the same way, as a stimulus meant to correct their idleness. Gill guards the charge: not all of them disobeyed, some hearkened, and perhaps by far the greater part.
22:
Whether the sabbath already existed is the chapter’s sharpest dispute, and it turns on this passage. Henry finds here a plain intimation that a seventh-day sabbath was observed not only before the law was given at Sinai but before Israel came out of Egypt, and therefore from the beginning. His argument is twofold. Had the sabbath been instituted only now, how could Moses have understood what God said about a double portion when no express mention of the sabbath was made? And how could the people take the hint so readily, even to their rulers’ surprise, before Moses had explained the reason, unless they knew of it already? Setting apart one day in seven was, he concludes, a divine appointment ever since man was created and the most ancient of positive laws. Wesley reproduces the whole argument almost sentence for sentence. Clarke takes the same side from the wording: nothing in text or context suggests the sabbath was now first given, and it is spoken of as perfectly well known from general observance — though he allows the commandment may be here renewed, since the people might have thought their unsettled state exempted them. He arranges the history in three stages: instituted when creation was finished, insisted on when the people came out of Egypt, and made a tenth part of the whole when the Law was given.

Ellicott contradicts them on grammatical grounds and concedes their case only to withdraw it. If the English were correct, he says, the previous institution of the sabbath and the people’s knowledge of it would be necessarily implied, since nothing else explains the double use of the article; but the Hebrew has no article here or below, and its absence indicates a new thing announced, if not absolutely then at least to those who hear it. He grants that much may be said for a primeval institution and that Babylonian observance favours its being known to Abraham’s family; but continued observance would have been impossible under the oppression, and the elders’ surprise with the words of Moses show the idea was then practically a novelty.

Clarke argues the miracle from the same arrangement. What convinced him was the pattern: none fell on the seventh day, which no natural production would have observed, and what was laid up for that day did not corrupt though it infallibly corrupted overnight on any other. God showed his power three ways at once — sending it on six days, withholding it on the seventh, and preserving it for that one day alone. Ellicott adds that the directions to bake and to seethe imply a substance unlike any natural manna, since the gift could be made into a paste and baked or turned into porridge.

Calvin reads the rulers’ report as evidence of unbelief rather than diligence. They had heard from Moses that God would give two days’ provision, and still they marvel and report it as strange and incredible; they obeyed and did not spare their labour, but their astonishment at seeing God perform what he promised betrays them, since they credited his word only when its truth was proved to their eyes. Yet their doubting served, by God’s wisdom, both to confirm the miracle and to establish the sabbath, giving Moses occasion to enjoin a rest they might otherwise have neglected. Ellicott reads the surprise more charitably, that Moses either had not passed on the earlier announcement or that they had failed to understand it. Henry draws a rule from the baking done a day early: the strictness does not make it unlawful now to dress meat on the Lord’s day, but directs us to arrange our affairs so they hinder us as little as possible in the work of the day. Gill notes that what was laid up was the remainder of two omers a man, neither baked nor boiled.
25:
Ellicott takes the words on this day as the moment of institution, or of re-institution, after which the sabbath became binding on Israel. Its essential character as a weekly rest was assigned to it at once, he argues, by three things together: by the name given it, which simply means a rest; by God’s own resting from the self-imposed task of giving the manna; and by the rest which the absence of manna on the seventh day imposed on the people, who could do nothing but stay in and eat what they had. In this way, he says, the ground was prepared for the stringent law of sabbath observance afterwards laid down in the fourth commandment. The reading is deliberately careful: he will not say whether it was instituted or restored, but he will say that from this point it was binding.

Gill keeps to the narrative. Moses spoke on the seventh day in the morning and told them to eat what they had, baked or boiled or just as it was, whichever they pleased; and he adds the reason they had no choice about the day itself, since none fell on it. On the standing rule he is equally brief: they were to gather it day after day, every morning, as they had done for the six days past, and so throughout their stay in the wilderness.

The going out on the seventh day Calvin calls the second transgression, and reads it as a direct charge of falsehood against Moses. By going out they trenched on the day’s religious observance, and the monstrous greediness that drove them arose from simply not believing what Moses had just said, since he had plainly told them they would find nothing; refusing to credit anything but their own eyes, they in effect accused him of lying. Meanwhile the obligation of the sabbath was set at nought, and worse, they sought to profane a day God had hallowed so that it should differ in no way from the rest.

Calvin then notices to whom the rebuke is addressed and why. God inveighs against them with much bitterness, but speaks to Moses, arraigning in his person the obstinate wickedness of the whole people. Moses was certainly not among those who had refused to obey; yet by a general charge the transgressing multitude is more severely rebuked, and a greater obligation is laid on Moses to chastise them when a part of the blame is transferred to himself. In the words how long? Calvin hears God declaring the sheer intolerableness of their perversity, since there is no end to their offences and they prove themselves incorrigible by provoking greater vengeance with new crimes. Gill supposes the incident happened perhaps on the very next seventh day.
28:
The rebuke is aimed at a second offence rather than the same one. Ellicott points out that the people had already broken one positive precept by hoarding, and now broke another at least in spirit, since they would have gathered had there been anything to find; so they provoked God a second time, and yet he did not destroy them but turned his anger away, apparently allowing for an ordinance so new they were not yet used to it. Gill has the Lord speaking out of the cloud, having seen and been displeased by the men who went into the field. Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the command forward.

The command to abide in one’s place has been taken with very different degrees of literalness, and both Clarke and Ellicott review the history of that. Clarke reads it as an instruction to stay home and give the time to religious exercises rather than go out for manna or anything else, and reports that several Jewish authorities understood place as the camp and fixed a limit of a thousand cubits, about an English mile, as the sabbath day’s journey, drawing the figure from the suburbs in Numbers. Ellicott gives the same rule at a different reckoning, six stadia, traditionally the extreme distance from the camp’s centre to its furthest boundary. He notes that some took the direction absolutely literally and stayed all day in whatever position they woke in, but says this adherence to the letter was generally repudiated and the command understood as forbidding men to leave the camp.

Clarke reports the same extreme literalism and cannot leave it alone. He tells of a rabbi who fell into a slough on a Saturday and refused to be pulled out, giving his reason in a Latin couplet; whereupon his Christian neighbours determined he should honour their sabbath in the same place and left him there all Sunday, answering in a couplet of their own. A grimmer version follows from an old chronicle, where a Jew who fell into a pit and would not be drawn out for reverence of the day was kept there by an earl until Monday, by which time he was found dead. His comment on the first is dry — it might have convinced the man of his folly, but was certainly not the likeliest way to convert him — and of the second he says plainly that the earl murdered him. Gill records the outcome plainly: the people rested, did not go out in quest of manna, kept the day as a rest from labour, and continued so in later generations.

On the name and the description the readers add detail. Gill says they had given it no name until now, which he takes against reading the earlier verse as it is manna rather than as a question, though he allows the name may have stuck because that was the first word they used. Ellicott corrects the form, the Greek shape of the word first appearing in the Septuagint of Numbers, and reconciles the two descriptions: hoar frost describes its look on the ground, coriander seed its appearance once collected. He compares the taste to the wafers Egyptians and Greeks used as offerings, of fine flour, oil and honey, and reports the tradition, found in the book of Wisdom, that the taste varied with the eater’s wish. Calvin reads both details as evidence. The form proves the miracle, since grains round and like coriander seed were nothing that had been seen before; and the taste convicts the people of ingratitude in rejecting a food not only appropriate and wholesome but very sweet. The name itself he takes as a testimony wrung from malicious and ungrateful men by the sheer conspicuousness of the thing, so that anyone who dares raise a question on so manifest a point stands condemned by it.
32:
All the readers notice that the narrative has left its order here. Gill says Moses spoke at another time and the passage is inserted to give the account of the manna all together. Calvin says the same and finds a purpose in it: by interposing these circumstances out of sequence Moses the more confirms that this food was created by God’s special bounty, since he wanted an omer preserved as a memorial which, undergoing no putrefaction, handed the miracle down to posterity. Keil and Delitzsch note the same anticipation, the placing of the jar being reported here so that everything of importance about the manna should be summed up in one place. Clarke simply refers the reader back to his earlier note on the difficulty of a testimony that did not yet exist.

What the pot was made of is settled by an appeal outside the chapter. Gill reports the options: a Targum and a rabbi call it earthen, another allows earthen or brass, brass being likelier for durability, and others take it for glass; but the Greek version makes it golden, a Jewish writer agrees and the apostle confirms it, which Gill says puts the matter beyond question. Keil and Delitzsch handle the word itself, deriving it from a root meaning to guard or preserve, so that it means a jar or bottle and not a basket; they too note that the Jerusalem Targum makes it earthenware while the Greek adds an adjective for gold that has nothing corresponding in the original.

Where it was laid is agreed and its significance disputed only in degree. Ellicott sets the two phrases side by side — before the Lord, and before the Testimony, that is the two tables — recalls that the Epistle to the Hebrews puts three things only in the ark, the tables, the pot of manna and the budded rod, and accounts for so sacred a deposit by the manna typifying the true bread from heaven. Gill places the pot beside the ark rather than within it, and reads the golden vessel as a figure of the word and ordinances that hold forth Christ, precious as gold and lasting until the second coming.

Henry reads the memorial as a piece of evidence for a future trial. Posterity was to see what the food was and how much the daily portion came to, so that it might appear they were kept neither to hard fare nor to short allowance, and might judge between God and Israel whether cause was ever given for murmuring. Eaten bread, he says, must not be forgotten. He notes the preservation itself as a standing miracle and therefore the fitter memorial, and marks how long the mercy lasted: it never ceased until they reached a land with bread enough and to spare, and though Israel was very provoking it never failed them, as God still causes his rain to fall on the just and the unjust.
34:
Clarke picks up a chronological difficulty in the placing. The Testimony properly belonged to the tabernacle, which was not yet built; and he takes the word itself to signify reference to something beyond itself, so that tabernacle, manna, tables and rod alike bore witness to a spiritual good still to come. Gill locates the pot beside the ark of the testimony rather than in it, and explains the name: the ark was called the testimony because it contained the law, which was a testification of God’s mind and will to Israel.

Wesley takes the memorial as an invitation to read the whole episode typically, and works the figure out at length. The manna is called spiritual meat because it typified spiritual blessings: Christ himself is the true manna and bread of life of which this was a figure, the word of God is the manna by which our souls are nourished, and the comforts of the Spirit are the hidden manna. These, he says, support the divine life while we are in the wilderness of this world; it was food for those only who followed the pillar of cloud and fire; and it had to be gathered, so that Christ in the word must be applied to the soul and every one of us must gather for himself. There was enough for all and enough for each and none had too much, so in Christ there is a complete sufficiency and no superfluity. But the comparison ends in a contrast: those who ate manna hungered again and died at last, and with many of them God was not well pleased, whereas those who feed on Christ by faith shall never hunger and shall die no more.

The forty years raise a question of authorship, and two answers are given. Clarke notes that the verse has been used to argue the book was not written until after the manna ceased, and answers that the words may have been added by Ezra, who collected and arranged the inspired books and supplied such connecting sentences as were needed, since before his time the books of the Old Testament were on the universal testimony of the Jews in an unconnected and scattered state. Ellicott keeps the verse for Moses. He may have added it shortly before his death, when the manna had continued for thirty-nine years and nine months; and the verse does not say the supply had ceased, which in fact it did not do until the Jordan was crossed under Joshua and Canaan actually reached. Gill reckons the period more exactly: forty years less thirty days from the passover in Egypt to the passover at Gilgal, the round number being given as is common.

The closing note on the omer is treated as a gloss by everyone who mentions it. Clarke says its true place seems to be several verses earlier, since where it stands it has no connection. Ellicott explains why it was needed: both measures were Egyptian, and while the ephah remained in use until the captivity the omer fell out very early, so this parenthetic explanation may have been added by whoever completed Deuteronomy or by a later editor. Gill uses it to show how ample the provision was, giving the rabbinic scale in eggshells and then a modern conversion, an ephah at seven gallons and a half and an omer at three quarts. Clarke closes with the conclusion he thinks the miracle establishes, that salvation is of the Lord: as Israel must have perished had God not fed them, so the manna was a type of the Redeemer and his salvation, an application Christ made of it himself.
